original_value: Research on the role of non-driving related tasks (NDRT) in the area of automated driving is indispensable. At the same time, the construct mode awareness has received considerable interest in regard to human–machine interface (HMI) evaluation. Based on the expectation that HMI design and practice with different levels of driving automation influence NDRT engagement, a driving simulator study was conducted. In a 2 × 5 (automation level x block) design, N = 49 participants completed several transitions of control. They were told that they could engage in an NDRT if they felt safe and comfortable to do so. The NDRT was the Surrogate Reference Task (SuRT) as a representative of a wide range of visual–manual NDRTs. Engagement (i.e., number of inputs on the NDRT interface) was assessed at the onset of a respective episode of automated driving (i.e., after transition) and during ongoing automation (i.e., before subsequent transition). Results revealed that over time, NDRT engagement increased during both L2 and L3 automation until stable engagement at the third block. This trend was observed for both onset and ongoing NDRT engagement. The overall engagement level and the increase in engagement are significantly stronger for L3 automation compared to L2 automation. These results outline the potential of NDRT engagement as an online non-intrusive measure for mode awareness. Moreover, repeated interaction is necessary until users are familiar with the automated system and its HMI to engage in NDRTs. These results provide researchers and practitioners with indications about users’ minimum degree of familiarity with driving automation and HMIs for mode awareness testing.

result.paraphrase: Research into the role of non-driving-related tasks (NDRT) in automated driving is essential. At the same time, the construct of mode awareness has drawn substantial attention in human–machine interface (HMI) evaluation. Assuming that HMI design and experience with different levels of driving automation affect NDRT engagement, a driving simulator study was carried out. Using a 2 × 5 design (automation level × block), 49 participants completed multiple transitions of control. They were informed that they could take part in an NDRT if they felt safe and comfortable doing so. The NDRT used was the Surrogate Reference Task (SuRT), representing a broad range of visual-manual NDRTs. Engagement, measured by the number of inputs on the NDRT interface, was evaluated at the start of each automated-driving episode (after transition) and during ongoing automation (before the next transition). The findings showed that NDRT engagement increased over time in both L2 and L3 automation until reaching stable levels in the third block, with this pattern appearing for both onset and ongoing engagement. Overall engagement and the growth in engagement were significantly greater under L3 automation than under L2 automation. These results indicate the potential of NDRT engagement as an online, non-intrusive measure of mode awareness. In addition, repeated interaction is needed until users are familiar with the automated system and its HMI enough to engage in NDRTs. The results offer researchers and practitioners guidance on users’ minimum familiarity with driving automation and HMIs for mode-awareness testing.
